ARIZONA GRADE 5 The Island Water Mystery
A survival story with a missing explanation

The Island Water Mystery

What happens to matter when it seems to disappear?

Theo has reached a part of his island survival book that should make sense, but it doesn’t. The story’s water trick seems to work, but the explanation is missing. There’s only one way to find out whether it really adds up: follow the evidence.

In this lesson, students investigate what happened to the water and salt in a solar still after a survival story leaves the explanation out. They establish starting measurements, observe a substance become impossible to see while its mass is unchanged, build and seal the story’s setup, track matter through a closed system along one of two evidence trails, and construct a model and an evidence-based explanation showing that the amount of matter stayed the same.

Learning objectives

1

Explain that matter can be made of pieces too small to see, using evidence from a substance that dissolves.

2

Analyze and interpret measurement data to determine whether the amount of matter changed.

3

Explain why the amount of matter stays the same in a closed system.

4

Track a substance through a system by gathering and combining evidence from more than one location.

5

Develop a model representing where matter went when it became difficult to see.

6

Communicate an evidence-based scientific explanation for an authentic audience.

Student-friendly learning goals

  • I can use measurements and observations to track matter even when I cannot see it.
  • I can analyze data to explain why the amount of matter stays the same in a closed system.
  • I can create a model showing what happened to the water and salt.

Standards & practices

📐 Arizona science standard

5.P1U1.1 — Analyze and interpret data to explain that matter of any type can be subdivided into particles too small to see and, in a closed system, if properties change or chemical reactions occur, the amount of matter stays the same.

🔬 Science & engineering practices

Planning and Carrying Out Investigations · Analyzing and Interpreting Data · Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking · Developing and Using Models · Constructing Explanations · Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information

🔗 Crosscutting concepts

Cause and Effect · Scale, Proportion, and Quantity · Systems and System Models · Energy and Matter

⭐ Stories in Science framework alignment

Students enter through a gap in a survival story, record an initial idea before any evidence, gather before-and-after measurements in a sealed system, choose an evidence trail (Track the Water vs. Track the Salt) while the complementary trail is investigated alongside them, converge both data sets into a single accounting of matter, revise their original thinking, build a particle model, and write an evidence-based explanation to the book’s author — then export an Investigation Journal artifact.

Instructional boundary: Students are not expected to distinguish mass from weight or explain evaporation, condensation, or chemical reactions at the atomic scale.
Story start

The part Theo read twice

Theo's finger stopped halfway down the page.

He read the same sentence out loud again.

“The family used the sun to turn ocean water into fresh water.”

Mom looked up from the kitchen table.

“You read that twice,” she said, a smile spreading across her face.

Theo tapped the sentence.

“Because it skipped something.”

From Theo's book

The Rivera Family — A Water Story

Theo turned the page, waiting for the part that explained it.

The family packed up. The chapter ended.

He flipped back, checking whether he had missed a paragraph somewhere. He hadn't. The story went straight from the setup to It worked — and never said why.

“That’s it?”

At the kitchen table

What did the story leave out?

Theo carried the open book to the kitchen table and slid it toward his mom.

“The story jumps straight from the setup to ‘It worked.’” He looked up. “You’re the chemist. Does that make sense to you?”

Mom studied the illustration.

“It does. But I think you can figure this one out.”

“Can’t you just tell me?”

Mom slid the book back toward him.

“I could. But where’s the fun in that? What does the story leave unanswered?”

Theo pointed at the container.

“The water around the cup got lower. Then water showed up inside the cup, and the cup started out empty.”

He tapped the first picture.

“But that ocean water was salty.”

So there were two things the story never explained.

💧

Where did the water go?

🧂

What happened to the salt?

Mom nodded toward the beginning and ending pictures.

“Good questions. What would you need to know to answer them?”

Plan the evidence

Think about what you might observe, measure, or compare. You do not need to know the answer yet.

✓ Saved

Theo looked at the two pictures for a long moment — the full container at the start, the fuller cup at the end.

“How much they started with. And how much they ended with.” He picked up the book again. “Otherwise there’s no way to tell where anything went.”

“We need evidence from before and after.”

Starting the trail

Start with the evidence

Mom cleared a space on the table.

“If you think something was left out, we start at the beginning,” she said. “And we keep track.”

Theo pulled his notebook closer.

“If we figure this out, I want to write to the author.”

Mom raised an eyebrow.

“About the story?”

“About the science,” Theo said. “The part the story skipped.”

Mom opened his notebook to a clean page.

“Then make sure your evidence can support whatever you end up telling them.”

Theo picked up his pencil.

Mom tapped the blank page.

“Start with what you think happened. Later, see what the evidence does to your idea.”

Before the evidence

This is your starting idea. There is no right answer yet — you will come back to it after you collect evidence.

✓ Saved
Theo’s notebook

The missing before

Mom cleared a space on the counter and set out the water, the salt, and a digital scale. Of course she'd have one of those, Theo thought.

He put his notebook down beside it and uncapped his pen.

“Before we change anything,” he said, “we need to know what we started with.”

Theo circled 255 g. “Now we know what we started with.” He pulled the clear container closer.

At the kitchen table

The first disappearance

Theo set the measured water and salt beside the container. “Same starting materials as the book.” Mom glanced at his notebook. “Then keep track of what changes.”

Evidence check

Use what you observed and measured. You do not need to use a science vocabulary word yet.

✓ Saved

Theo held the mixture to the light. “I can’t see the salt, but it’s still 255 grams.” Mom waited. Theo looked back at the book. “Then I can’t call it gone just because I can’t see it.”

Back to the book

Recreate the book’s setup

Theo propped the book beside the materials. “Now we copy their setup.” Mom pointed toward the scale. “Before it goes into the sun, what will you need?” Theo nodded. “The whole thing—sealed.”

Theo recorded 595 g. The cup was empty and the setup was sealed. “That’s our before.” He carried it toward the sunny window.

At the windowsill

A day in the sun

Theo set the sealed setup in the sunlight. Mom smiled. “Now the hard part: wait and watch.” Theo checked his notebook one more time: 595 g.

Evidence check

Think about where the water appears to be and what the scale tells you about the whole system.

✓ Saved

The scale settled at 595 g again. Theo stared at the water in the cup. “Same total. Different places.” He looked back at the saltwater. “But I still can’t account for everything.” Mom nodded toward his notebook. “Then what still needs evidence?”

Evidence checkpoint

Two evidence trails

Theo looked from the water in the collection cup to the mixture left in the container.

“The total didn’t change,” he said. “But I still can’t account for the water or the salt.”

Mom pulled his notebook closer.

“Then don’t try to answer both questions at once.”

Theo drew a line down the page.

Where did the water go?
Where is the salt now?

Following one trail

Track the water

Theo looked at the 595 g measurement he had circled after the setup came out of the sun. “Now we can open it,” Mom said. Theo lifted the clear cover and looked from the water in the collection cup to the droplets above it and the mixture left in the container. “I’ll follow the water first.”

Theo wrote 147 g beside the cup and cover, then stopped at the 108 g remaining mixture. “I can measure that mixture, but I still can’t say how much of it is water.” Mom nodded. “Then one trail isn’t enough.”

Following one trail

Track the salt

Theo looked at the 595 g measurement he had circled after the setup came out of the sun. “Now we can open it,” Mom said. Theo set the collected water, the wet cover, and the remaining mixture where he could compare them. “If the salt is still here, the evidence should point somewhere.” Mom slid the tester across the table. “Then follow the evidence before you decide.”

Theo drew a box around the 18 g recovered salt and looked back at the three tester results. “That answers the salt question. But it still doesn’t tell me where all the water went.” Mom nodded toward the other side of the notebook. “Then one trail isn’t enough.”

Evidence comes together

Two trails, one system

Mom turned her notebook around.

“While you followed the water, I checked the salt evidence.”

Theo pulled the two sets of notes together.

“So neither trail had the whole answer.”

“Right,” Mom said. “Put them together.”

Mom turned her notebook around.

“While you followed the salt, I tracked the water.”

Theo pulled the two sets of notes together.

“So neither trail had the whole answer.”

“Right,” Mom said. “Put them together.”

THEO’S NOTES
Collection cup—
Clear cover—
Remaining mixture—
Water directly identified—
MOM’S NOTES
Collected waterNo detectable salt
Cover dropletsNo detectable salt
Remaining mixtureSalt detected
Recovered salt18 g

“The remaining 108 g is a mixture. Now we know 18 g of that mixture is salt.”

108 g remaining mixture − 18 g salt = g water

“Now account for the water in all three places.”

132 g in collection cup + 15 g on cover + 90 g remaining in mixture = g water

“Now put the water and salt back into one total.”

237 g water + 18 g salt = g

Starting water + salt 255 g → Accounted water + salt 255 g
Whole sealed setup, before sunlight 595 g → Whole sealed setup, after sunlight 595 g
What did combining the two evidence trails let you figure out?
✓ Saved

Theo read the numbers from top to bottom.

237 g of water. 18 g of salt. 255 g together.

“The numbers fit.”

Mom glanced toward the open survival book.

“Good. Now the harder question is why something can still be there when it becomes hard to see.”

Explaining the science

Look back at your first idea

Theo turned back to the page that started all of this and read the sentence one more time.

“They still never say why it works.”

Mom slid his notebook across the table, open to the very first page he had written on.

“You do now. Start with what you thought before you had any of this.”

Your first idea Written before you collected any evidence
Look back

Look back at what you originally thought. What would you change, add, or explain differently now? Two or three sentences are enough.

✓ Saved
Explaining the science

Build a model of the matter

Mom tapped the empty space below his numbers.

“Numbers show how much. A model shows where. Draw where everything ended up.”

Where did the matter end up?

Each group below stands for tiny pieces of matter — far too small to see on their own. Place each group where your evidence says it ended up. Tap a group, then tap a place — or drag it there.

Matter to place

Everything has been placed.

Inside the sealed setup
Clear cover 15 g water · no salt detected
Collection cup 132 g water · no salt detected
Remaining mixture 90 g water · 18 g salt detected
Outside the sealed setup The cover was never opened while it sat in the sun

Matter at the start 237 g water + 18 g salt = 255 g
Matter in your model 132 g + 15 g + 90 g water + 18 g salt = 255 g
Matter that left the sealed setup 0 g

Theo looked at the model he had just drawn, then back at the book.

“So the water never left. It just stopped being easy to see.”

Explaining the science

Write to the author

Theo set his model beside the survival book, still open to the page where the explanation should have been.

Mom handed him a fresh sheet of paper.

“Tell them what you found. In your own words, with your evidence behind it.”

Your letter to the author

Use your own evidence — your measurements, your salt-test results, or your model. This is the explanation the book was missing.

✓ Saved
Case closed

Mystery solved

Theo signed his name at the bottom and read the whole thing back to himself.

“That’s the part the story left out,” Mom said. “And you found it yourself.”

Theo picked up the survival book one more time. The same sentence was still there, still skipping the explanation — but it read differently now.

🔎

You followed the evidence, changed your thinking when the evidence called for it, built a model, and explained the part the survival story skipped.

The water never disappeared. It just went somewhere he hadn’t learned to look yet.

Glossary

Matter
Anything that takes up space and has weight.
System
The objects and materials being studied together.
Closed system
A system in which matter cannot enter or leave.

Investigation Journal

Fills in as you work through the investigation.
